property_summary: Calls to withdraw succeed (do not revert) only when msg.sender is the contract's Owner; i.e., non-owners' withdraw calls must revert.

For any caller who is the Owner and any contract balance, calling withdraw() always sends the entire contract balance to Owner (so address(c).balance == 0 afterwards); the mutant that transfers to msg.sender instead can leave funds in the contract when Owner != msg.sender, violating this.

For any caller who is the contract Owner and for any nonzero contract balance, calling withdraw() always empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that sends to msg.sender instead of Owner can leave funds in the contract when Caller (msg.sender) differs from Owner, so the property fails for some inputs.

For any caller and any contract balance, if withdraw() is invoked by the recorded Owner, the contract's balance becomes zero afterwards (the Owner always receives the full balance); the mutant sending to msg.sender can leave funds in the contract when msg.sender != Owner, violating this.

For any caller address that is the recorded Owner and any incoming prior balance, after Owner calls withdraw() the contract balance becomes zero (Owner always receives the full balance); the mutant that transfers to msg.sender instead can leave funds in the contract when Owner != msg.sender, so there exist fuzzed inputs (different msg.sender vs Owner with funds present) that make address(c).balance != 0 in the mutant.

For every caller who is the contract Owner, after Owner calls withdraw() the Owner's address must receive the contract balance (so Owner's external balance increases by address(c).balance prior to the call); the mutant sending to msg.sender can send funds to a different EOA (msg.sender) when Owner is a contract, violating the property when Owner is a contract account that cannot receive (or diverts funds), so there exist fuzzed inputs showing the mutant fails to deliver funds to Owner.

For any caller who is the Owner and any contract balance, calling withdraw() transfers the entire contract balance to Owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that transfers 0 breaks this by leaving balance > 0 for some inputs.

For any caller who is the Owner and for any positive contract balance funded by Owner, calling withdraw() empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that transfers 0 leaves a non-zero balance for some such inputs.

For any owner-triggered withdrawal after the contract has positive balance, calling withdraw() empties the contract (address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that transfers 0 can leave a non-zero balance, so the property will fail for some funded inputs.

For any caller (owner) and any nonzero contract balance, calling withdraw() results in the contract balance becoming zero; the mutant that transfers 0 can leave a nonzero balance and thus violates this rule for some inputs.

For any caller that is the Owner and any initial contract balance funded by a third-party addr, after Owner calls withdraw the reference contract forwards all ether it holds to Owner (so address(c).balance == 0), while the mutant that transfers 0 can leave nonzero balance for some funded inputs — we restrict to the case where Owner is not the funder to ensure funds move between distinct parties.

For any caller and any contract balance, when Owner calls withdraw the contract's balance becomes zero (all funds transferred to Owner); the mutant that calls transfer twice can revert or fail to make this true for some inputs (double transfer attempts can revert or leave non-zero balance).

For any caller who is the Owner and any initial contract balance, a single call to withdraw always drains the contract balance to zero in the reference; the mutant that attempts a double transfer can revert or leave a non-zero contract balance for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any contract balance, calling withdraw succeeds (does not revert) and leaves the contract balance equal to zero in the reference; the mutant which issues two transfers to Owner can cause the call to revert for some inputs (e.g. when the first transfer drains balance so the second transfer reverts), thus violating the universal success property.

For any Owner address and any nonzero initial contract balance, a call to withdraw by Owner will always transfer at most the contract balance once and thus will never cause a revert when Owner is a normal externally-owned account; the mutant that issues two transfers can cause a revert when Owner is a contract whose payable receive() reverts on a second transfer attempt (the reference never reverts for such an Owner because only one transfer is attempted).

For any owner address that may reject the second incoming transfer (i.e., an owner contract whose receive() reverts after accepting one payment) and any funded contract balance/withdraw caller being Owner, the reference C never reverts and leaves address(c).balance == 0 after withdraw succeeds, while the mutant that performs two transfers can cause withdraw to revert or leave a nonzero contract balance for some fuzzed funding amount and owner contract behavior; we assert that when Owner is a contract that accepts a single transfer then reverts on the second, calling withdraw succeeds (does not revert) and empties the contract in the reference but the mutant will fail for some fuzzed value — we use a helper OwnerThatRevertsOnSecond to demonstrate this.
Calling Command with nonzero msg.value forwards that value to target address (observable as increase in target balance), i.e., when caller sends value, target balance increases by that value.

property_summary: Calling Command with a nonzero attached value never reverts (i.e., when the caller sends ether with the call, the call completes).
If a nonzero amount is sent to Command, the call does not revert (i.e., amount == 0 || reverted == false).
In the original contract, sending a nonzero amount does not cause Command to revert.
In the original contract, sending a nonzero amount to Command does not cause it to revert (i.e., amount == 0 || reverted == false).

For any caller and any calldata, when Owner calls Command forwarding nonzero ETH, the reference contract forwards that ETH to the target (call succeeds or fails but accepts value); the mutant forbids any nonzero msg.value and thus reverts when Owner sends value, so there exist inputs (Owner sending >0 value) where mutant behavior differs.
Calling Command with non-owner must revert OR, when called by the owner, it must not revert even if the callee reverts (i.e., owner-invoked Command never causes the transaction to revert).

For any caller and any calldata/value, when the Owner calls Command forwarding some ETH, the contract C forwards the same ETH value to the target (so the call succeeds with value and may transfer ETH) — the mutant using staticcall disallows value transfer, so for some calldata/value the mutant will behave differently (the call will not forward ETH and may fail or not transfer funds).

For any caller and any msg.value, when the Owner calls Command(addr,data) with value X, the reference forwards that value X to the callee (so the callee's payable fallback/receive gets X and address(c).balance decreases accordingly), whereas the mutant that strips the value breaks this by not forwarding Ether; thus the property: after Owner calls Command(attacker, data) with value X, the reference always results in address(c).balance reduced by X (callee receives X) while the buggy version can leave address(c).balance unchanged for some inputs.

For any caller Owner and any sent ETH value v, when Owner calls Command(attacker, data) the reference forwards the full v so c's balance decreases by v (callee receives v), whereas the mutant that strips value can leave c's balance unchanged for some inputs (the adversarial callee only accepts value when forwarded).

If Owner calls Command(target,data) with some nonzero msg.value and the target contract's fallback/receive reverts when it receives nonzero Ether, then the correct contract always forwards the Ether causing the call to revert (so Command invocation reverts), whereas the mutant that strips value can succeed (not revert) for the same inputs; the property asserts that Command call always reverts for any nonzero value when the callee is a reverter helper.

If Owner calls Command(target,data) with msg.value == 0 then both versions behave the same (call succeeds or fails identically); in particular, for any address and calldata when msg.value == 0 the Command call must NOT change c.balance (it remains equal to address(c).balance) — the mutant that drops forwarded value still preserves behavior for zero value, so we assert that Command does not alter c.balance when called with zero value (this holds for reference for all inputs and the mutant will violate it when inputs include nonzero value, so we restrict to zero to make reference hold universally while mutant still fails on some inputs if fuzzed differently).

For any caller who is Owner and any nonzero ETH amount v, if the callee's fallback accepts payable calls by recording received value into its public storage, then after Owner calls Command(callee, data) paying v the reference contract always results in the callee having received v (and c's balance decreased by v), whereas the mutant that drops msg.value can leave the callee's recorded received value at 0 for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller and any value x sent with Command to a callee, the reference contract forwards exactly the msg.value x (so address(c).balance decreases by x) or succeeds without forwarding more than msg.value; the mutant sometimes forwards the entire contract balance instead, causing address(c).balance to drop by more than msg.value (violating the exact-forwarding rule).

For any caller and any Ether value v sent to Command, the original contract forwards exactly v to the callee (so address(c).balance decreases by at most v); the mutant sometimes forwards the entire contract balance instead, making address(c).balance drop by more than the sent v.

For any caller and any ether value sent to Command, the original contract forwards exactly the msg.value to the callee (so address(c).balance decreases by at most the sent msg.value when the callee reverts), while the mutant can forward the entire contract balance causing a larger balance decrease when the callee reverts; we detect this by using a callee that reverts on receive so the mutated extra-forwarding changes whether Command succeeds and/or changes c's balance.

For any caller and any msg.value sent to Command, if the callee's fallback always succeeds (does not revert) then after Command returns the contract's balance has decreased by exactly msg.value (the reference forwards only msg.value), whereas the mutant can forward the entire contract balance making the decrease larger than msg.value.

For any owner-invoked Command sending msg.value to a callee whose fallback is payable and records received amount, the reference forwards exactly msg.value (so address(c).balance decreases by msg.value and the callee's recorded received equals msg.value); the mutant may forward the entire contract balance, causing the callee to observe/receive more than msg.value (violating the equality).
